passage: The corridor outside Class 5 was roaring before the bell, and Anand Sir had five minutes to find out whose pencil box was left open. He asked Parveen, "Did you see it? Eyes on me while I am talking." Parveen's eyes stayed on the floor. At home, Dadi always said that meeting an elder's eyes is rude. Anand Sir's voice sharpened, and Parveen's throat closed. Then the bell rang and the noise faded. Anand Sir crouched and asked, "Tell me why you look down." Parveen explained. "In my class, looking at me shows you're listening," said Anand Sir. "At home, looking down shows respect. Both are kind." They agreed on a quick glance at the start, then a nod.

qa.q: What did Dadi always say to Parveen?
qa.a: Dadi always said that meeting an elder's eyes is rude.

qa.q: What was Parveen feeling when the teacher asked for eye contact?
qa.a: Frightened and stuck; Parveen's throat closed and the eyes stayed on the floor out of respect.

qa.q: What could help Parveen and Anand Sir understand each other next time?
qa.a: A quick glance at the start and then a nod, which they agreed together.

qa.q: How might Anand Sir have read Parveen's lowered eyes at first?
qa.a: As not listening or hiding something, until Parveen explained it was respect.

grounding: A child taught not to meet an elder's eyes meets a teacher who asks for eye contact, and patient translation follows.

passage: On the morning of the school science fair, Dhruv practised the talk in front of Manjula Ma'am in a Mumbai classroom. Dhruv spoke to the floor. "Look at the judges, Dhruv," said Manjula Ma'am. "It shows confidence." Dhruv's voice shrank. Later, at the dinner table, Dhruv told Mummy. "Nani says looking straight at an elder is bad manners." Mummy thought and said, "At home Nani is right for us. On the stage, Ma'am is right for the judges. You are learning two ways of showing respect." The next day Dhruv looked at the judges for a moment, then at the model, then again at the judges, and won a small ribbon.

qa.q: Where did Dhruv practise the talk?
qa.a: Dhruv practised in front of Manjula Ma'am in a classroom.

qa.q: How did Dhruv feel when Manjula Ma'am asked for eye contact, and why?
qa.a: Uncomfortable and torn; the voice shrank because looking at adults felt rude at home.

qa.q: What did Mummy do that helped Dhruv?
qa.a: Mummy explained that both Nani and Ma'am are right in their own places, so Dhruv could use each without shame.

qa.q: How does Manjula Ma'am see eye contact on the stage?
qa.a: As a sign of confidence in front of the judges.

grounding: A child taught that looking an elder in the eye is rude meets a teacher who wants eye contact, and an adult translates.

passage: Keerthana, you look down when your teacher talks? Come, let your Kishore Thatha tell you. When I was nine, in Madurai, my father taught me never to stare into an elder's eyes. It was cheeky, he said. So when I went to the new mission school, I kept my eyes on my feet. Mr D'Costa, the English teacher, said, "Eyes up while I am speaking, boy." I couldn't. My neck would not lift. He thought I was hiding something. I thought he wanted me to be rude. I went home and cried. My father went with me the next morning. The two men talked for a long time. After that, Mr D'Costa would say, "Just look at my nose, Kishore." And my father said, "In his class, looking is listening." Both were right, you see.

qa.q: Where did Kishore go to school when he was nine?
qa.a: To the new mission school in Madurai.

qa.q: How did young Kishore feel when Mr D'Costa asked him to look up?
qa.a: He felt confused and upset, stuck between his father's rule and the teacher's request, and cried when he went home.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Thatha's story?
qa.a: His father going to the school the next morning to talk with Mr D'Costa, so both adults could explain their meanings to each other and to Kishore.

qa.q: How did Mr D'Costa first see Kishore's lowered eyes?
qa.a: He thought Kishore was hiding something, reading lowered eyes as dishonesty rather than respect.

grounding: It illustrates a child taught that meeting an elder's eyes is rude, who meets a teacher expecting eye contact and needs adults to translate.

passage: Kalyani's first day at the school in Dubai was loud: a fire drill, a new timetable and thirty children talking at once. When Mr Vishal, the class teacher, asked her name, she answered to the floor, as she did with elders at home. "Kalyani, look at me when you speak," he said, quite kindly. The class went quiet. Kalyani felt her face burn. Looking at a teacher's eyes felt like talking back. She tried, but her eyes slid away to his watch. At pickup she told her mother, and her mother wrote a short note in her diary. The next day Mr Vishal crouched beside her desk. "In your family, looking down is polite, yes? Here, looking up helps me know you're listening. You can look at my chin to start." Kalyani tried his chin. It was easier.

qa.q: What did Mr Vishal suggest Kalyani could look at to start?
qa.a: He suggested she could look at his chin to start.

qa.q: Why did Kalyani's face burn when Mr Vishal asked her to look at him?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and uneasy, because at home looking into an elder's eyes felt like talking back, and the class had gone quiet.

qa.q: How did Mr Vishal support Kalyani?
qa.a: He explained both meanings, looking down at home and looking up in class, and gave her an easier first step of looking at his chin.

qa.q: How might Kalyani's mother have felt reading about the first day?
qa.a: She was probably concerned for Kalyani and wanted the teacher to understand, so she wrote a note to explain.

grounding: It illustrates a child raised to lower her eyes before elders who meets a teacher expecting eye contact, and the patient translation between the two.

passage: Binita's Dadi had one rule she repeated at every visit: "Don't stare at elders, it's rude." So Binita, eight, looked at the floor when Dadi's friends spoke. In the new term at her Bengaluru school, Ojas sir took maths. On Monday he said, "Binita, eyes here, please," tapping his own eye. She lifted her face for a second, then dropped it. On Wednesday he said it again, more firmly. Binita's stomach knotted. Was she bad at home or bad at school? That evening she asked Dadi, who laughed softly. On Friday, Dadi wrote a note for Ojas sir. He read it, then knelt by her. "At home, lower eyes are respect. Here, looking at me tells me you're following. You're not being rude to anyone." Binita looked at him, just long enough to nod.

qa.q: What did Ojas sir tap when he said "eyes here, please"?
qa.a: He tapped his own eye.

qa.q: What was Binita worried about when Ojas sir asked again?
qa.a: She was anxious and confused, her stomach knotting, worried she was bad at home or bad at school.

qa.q: Which step helped most, and why?
qa.a: Dadi's note and Ojas sir kneeling to explain both meanings, because it showed Binita she was not being rude in either place.

qa.q: How might Ojas sir have seen Binita's lowered eyes at first?
qa.a: He may have thought she was not paying attention or was being shy, before the note helped him understand.

grounding: It illustrates a child taught that looking at elders is rude who meets a teacher asking for eye contact, and the patient translation between the two.

passage:
"Dilnaz, look at me when I'm speaking," Ms. Madhuri said.
Dilnaz kept her eyes on the teacher's sandals. "Sorry, Miss."
"I'm not angry. I just want to know you're listening."
"I am listening. My Dadi says it's rude to stare at elders. You keep your eyes down to show respect."
Ms. Madhuri crouched so they were the same height. "Ah. So at home, eyes down means respect."
"Yes."
"In this classroom, eyes up means 'I'm with you'. Both are respectful. They just speak different languages."
Dilnaz peeked up, then down again. "Can I look at your nose? That's in between."
Ms. Madhuri laughed. "The nose is perfect. And at home, keep doing what Dadi taught you."

qa.q: Who told Dilnaz that staring at elders is rude?
qa.a: Her Dadi told her that.

qa.q: What was Dilnaz feeling when asked to look up?
qa.a: Dilnaz felt confused and a little anxious, caught between Dadi's rule and the teacher's request.

qa.q: What did Ms. Madhuri do well?
qa.a: She stayed calm, asked why, and translated between the two meanings instead of calling Dilnaz rude.

qa.q: How might Ms. Madhuri have first read Dilnaz's lowered eyes?
qa.a: At first the teacher may have wondered whether Dilnaz was listening, before learning that at home it signals respect.

grounding: It illustrates a child taught that eye contact with elders is rude who meets a teacher expecting it, and the patient translation between the two meanings.
